outcome_intro: Running DNSFilter for a book of clients? Ask your AI "why is this site blocked for Acme Dental," "which unblock requests are waiting across my clients," or "who is still on the roaming client build that got pulled" and get one answer instead of clicking through each organization. why-blocked names the policy and rule that decided it, allow previews the fix on the policies that actually blocked it, and the fleet views cover every client org.

instead_of_say.instead: Opening the client's organization in the DNSFilter dashboard, finding which policy its site or roaming client uses right now, then reading the Query Log to work out which rule blocked the site the user is calling about
instead_of_say.say: Why is example.com blocked for Acme Dental, and which policy did it?

instead_of_say.instead: Working through end-user unblock requests one client at a time, looking up each domain's category and checking whether it is already allowed before deciding
instead_of_say.say: What unblock requests are waiting across my clients, and which are threats or already allowed?

instead_of_say.instead: After a roaming client release is pulled, filtering the Roaming Clients page organization by organization to find the machines still on that version
instead_of_say.say: Which clients still have Windows roaming clients on version 1.7.15?

pain_points: A blocked-site call is a chain, not a lookup. The answer depends on which policy the client's site or roaming client is using at that moment (scheduled policies change it by the quarter hour), that policy's allow list, block list and blocked categories, and what the Query Log recorded. A DNSFilter Community post, "Policy enforcement & reporting discrepancies with Roaming Client", describes a roaming client on a second site ignoring its category blocks, and reaching a URL that its reports showed as blocked.

Roaming client releases go wrong across the whole book at once. DNSFilter's own status page logged the Windows Roaming Client 1.7.15 auto-upgrade incident: auto-upgrade was paused, the release was pulled from general availability, and the workaround was to uninstall and reinstall the client. DNSFilter's help center also documents macOS machines losing internet connectivity when updating the Roaming Client from 1.x to 2.2. The first question each time is which clients, and which machines, are on the bad build.

Unblock requests and allow-list changes pile up per client. Each request means checking the domain's category, whether some policy or Universal List already allows it, and which policy to edit, and an allow added to the wrong policy (or a shared global one) opens the site for clients who never asked.

different_vs_wrappers: A plain DNSFilter API wrapper answers one endpoint per call, so "why is this blocked" turns into the AI chaining an organization lookup, site and roaming-client policy assignments, the current scheduled-policy slot, the policy's lists and categories, a domain lookup and the Query Log on its own. why-blocked and allow do that chain in one command and say what they could not evaluate. agents drift, agents stale and lists where answer from a local SQLite mirror that sync fills, so a fleet-wide question is one local query across every client org.
different_vs_vendor: It complements the DNSFilter dashboard rather than replacing it: policies, deployments, reporting and the Query Log stay there, while this skill brings cross-client troubleshooting, the unblock queue, roaming client drift and preview-first allow-list changes to whichever AI agent you already use.

faqs.a: Yes, on paid ChatGPT plans. ChatGPT connects to remote MCP servers over HTTPS, and dnsfilter-mcp speaks HTTP natively: run `dnsfilter-mcp --transport http` with DNSFILTER_MCP_HTTP_TOKEN set (it serves `http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp` and requires that token as a bearer header) and put it behind an HTTPS gateway that ChatGPT can sign in to with OAuth and that adds that bearer header, since ChatGPT connectors do not send a fixed one. Step-by-step in the install guide.

faqs.q: Do I need to know how to code?
faqs.a: No. Paste one sentence into Claude Code or Codex and your agent does the install, or run a one-line installer. You enter your credentials once.

Your data stays on your machine. The CLI, MCP server, and the local mirror are all local. The AI sees query results, not raw bulk data, and credentials are never bundled or transmitted by MSP Skills. Secret fields DNSFilter returns, such as each site's secret key and API key tokens, are not written to the local mirror.

faqs.q: What DNSFilter API key do I need?
faqs.a: An API token created in the DNSFilter dashboard (see DNSFilter's API Tokens help article). Set DNSFILTER_API_KEY to the token itself: DNSFilter expects the bare token in the Authorization header, with no Bearer prefix. Create it in your MSP organization so the cross-client commands can see your client organizations; a token from a single client organization only sees that client.

faqs.q: Can the AI allow a domain or change a policy by itself?
faqs.a: Only if you let it. allow prints the plan and writes nothing unless you add --confirm with a --note (the ticket number), refuses a domain in a security category unless you add --force, skips policies you cannot edit and leaves shared global policies alone unless you pass --include-global; a saved profile can never supply --confirm or --force. Generated commands such as policies update or policies add-whitelist-domain send as soon as they run, so preview them with --dry-run. Over MCP, the generic dnsfilter_execute tool can call any DNSFilter endpoint, deletes included, gated only by your AI app's approval prompt. For an agent that should only read, set DNSFILTER_MCP_READ_ONLY=1 in the MCP server's environment: write tools and allow are removed, dnsfilter_execute runs GET endpoints only, and API key reads, site secret keys and the roaming client uninstall PIN are withheld. Keep the approval prompt on.

faqs.q: Does why-blocked see every rule DNSFilter applies?
faqs.a: No, and it says so. It evaluates the site or roaming client's current policy (including the scheduled-policy slot and a roaming client inheriting its site's policy) in DNSFilter's documented order: allow list, allow-list-only mode, block list, uncategorized domains, blocked categories. User, collection and LAN-subnet assignments, the org or MSP Universal Allow and Block Lists, and AppAware application rules are not exposed by the policy API, so they are not evaluated; when a Query Log hit names a policy outside the ones it checked, the output flags it.

faqs.q: Why do agents drift, agents stale or lists where say there is nothing to report?
faqs.a: They read the local mirror, so run sync first: `dnsfilter-cli sync --full --resources organizations,networks,policies,scheduled-policies,user-agents`. agents drift also reads DNSFilter's release feed live on every run, so a pulled release does not linger in a stale copy.

faqs.q: Has it been tested against a live DNSFilter account?
faqs.a: Not yet. It is built from DNSFilter's published OpenAPI spec and tested against a local mock, so it ships as Beta and Awaiting live verification. A few request shapes were inferred from the spec (some list filters sent in the request body, the bulk domain lookup requiring fqdns) and will be confirmed on the first live run; tell us what you see.
Free. Apache-2.0 licensed. You pay only for whichever AI agent you already use.

governance_summary: The skill authenticates with a DNSFilter API token you create, and it can do whatever that token can do in the dashboard. Every troubleshooting and fleet view (why-blocked, unblocks triage, agents drift, agents stale, lists where, policy-audit) and the ordinary lists and gets are read-only and safe to let an agent run. allow previews by default; it and every policy, allow-list, block-list, scheduled-policy and unblock-decision change, and every change to which policy or bypass domains a site, MAC address or roaming client uses, need a human to approve the exact command, because one allow opens the site for every site and roaming client on that policy. Reads that return a secret (site secret keys in the networks lists, API key tokens, the roaming client uninstall PIN) and everything that creates, rotates or revokes a credential are human-only, as are deletes, roaming client uninstalls, billing, seat and distributor changes. The MCP server's generic execute tool can call any endpoint, so set DNSFILTER_MCP_READ_ONLY=1 for an agent that should only read.
